To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the transport of glucose and other hexoses across the blood-brain-barrier was decreased by about 1/3, and that the transport of neutral and basic amines and beta-hydroxy-butyrate was unaffected, in rats with experimental diabetes mellitus.

chronic hyperglycaemia decreases the number (not the affinity) of the glucose carrier molecules in the blood-brain-barrier, and that this adaptation is specific for glucose and not shared with other hexoses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the transport of glucose and amino acids across the blood-brain-barrier in diabetes mellitus.
the regulation of glucose transport across the blood-brain interface in normal and pathologic states, and with the effects of glucose transport on the brain.
the transport of nutrients and other substances into the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
diabetes is a metabolic disease that affects the transport of metabolic substrates across the blood-brain-barrier, which in turn affects the brain metabolism of these substrates.

the transport system for glucose across the BBB is downregulated by sustained hyperglycemic exposure, which is a characteristic of diabetes mellitus, and that the transport system is not downregulated in the presence of insulin deficiency alone.
diabetes mellitus is a disease of carbohydrate metabolism and the brain is not spared.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chronic hyperglycaemia, whether due to diabetes mellitus or starvation, causes an adaptive decrease in the number (not the affinity) of the hexose carrier proteins at the blood-bran barrier.
the blood-brain glucose transport is decreased in diabetes mellitus.
chronic hyperglycaemia decreases the number available of hexose carrier molecule at the blood-bran barrier.
The main takeaway from our work is that

chronic hyperglycaemia decreases the number available of high-affinity hexose carriers at the blood brain barrier, which could operate to decrease net flux of glucose in the brain during hyperglycaemia.
the blood-brain glucose transport is reduced in diabetes and that this reduction is probably due to a decrease in the amount of glucose transporters at the blood-brains barrier.
the brain can be affected by diabetes, and that it may be a contributing factor to some of the complications of diabetes, such as dementia.
